title: Purpose of the quality practice and product-based quality
blurb: Explain what the quality practice is for and why PRINCE2 anchors quality on the products the project delivers.
question: Which statement describes the purpose of the quality practice?

teach.h: What the quality practice is for
teach.body: Formally: the quality practice documents the user's requirements of the project's products and establishes the means by which those requirements will be met. In plain English: write down what the users need each product to be like, then set up how the project will build and check products so they really are like that. Quality is what makes the products usable, and usable products are what let the benefits happen.

steps.label:

teach.caption: The practice covers both what is required and how the project will make sure it is achieved.

teach.body: PRINCE2 defines quality as the degree to which the inherent characteristics of something (a product, service, process, person, organization, system or resource) fulfil its requirements. So quality is not 'luxury' or 'the best possible'. A basic product that meets its agreed requirements is a quality product; a gold-plated one that misses them is not.

PRINCE2 takes a product-based approach to requirements: it translates them into acceptance criteria and quality specifications for the project's products and the activities that deliver them. Every quality specification and quality check traces back to a product, and every product traces back to the business justification. That traceability stops resources being spent on work nobody can link to the reason for the project.

teach.caption: If a piece of work cannot be traced to a product and so to the justification, question why it is being done.

teach.body: However carefully requirements are captured in product descriptions during initiation, the project management team should expect them to change and be ready to handle those changes. Expecting requirements to stay fixed is unrealistic. Changes to baselined products are handled through the issues practice, so the quality practice and change control work together.

head: Practice
Purpose in short
rows: User's requirements of the products and how they will be met
What products, and who, how, where, when and how much
Collect and assess issues; control changes to the baseline
teach.caption: Exam distractors often swap these purposes. Quality is the one about requirements of the products.

teach.body: Fenmoor Council is replacing its library booking system. Project manager Tomasz Wilk sits down with the senior user, head of libraries Grace Oduya, to record what borrowers and staff need: renewals in three taps, screen reader support, overnight catalogue updates. Each requirement is tied to a product and a check. When a developer suggests building a social feed 'because it would be nice', Tomasz asks which product and which benefit it supports. It traces to neither, so it is not added.

teach.text: Classic traps: (1) Defining the products and the means to deliver them for the business case is the purpose of the PLANS practice, not quality. (2) Quality is not 'the highest standard'; it is meeting requirements. (3) Requirements are not expected to stay unchanged once captured.

items: Purpose: document the user's requirements of the products and establish how they will be met.
Quality = how far inherent characteristics fulfil requirements.
Product-based: requirements become acceptance criteria and quality specifications for products.
Traceability to the business justification avoids wasted work.
Expect requirements to change and handle the changes.

summary: You can now state the purpose of the quality practice and explain PRINCE2's definition of quality. You can also explain how product-based quality links every check to a product and to the business justification.

A.q: Which is the purpose of the quality practice?
options: To identify, assess and control uncertainties that would affect objectives
To define the products to be delivered and the means to deliver them
To collect and assess issues and control changes to the baseline
To document the user's requirements of the products and how they are met
A.why: The quality practice documents the user's requirements of the project's products and establishes the means by which they will be met (manual 8.1).

whyNot.0: This is the purpose of the risk practice.
whyNot.1: This is the purpose of the plans practice, which defines the what, who, how, where and when.
whyNot.2: This is the purpose of the issues practice.

options: The degree to which inherent characteristics fulfil requirements
The highest standard a supplier can achieve within the budget
The extent to which a product exceeds the user's expectations
The level of approval a product receives from the project board members
A.why: Quality is the degree to which a set of inherent characteristics of a product, service, process, person, organization, system or resource fulfils its requirements.

whyNot.1: Quality is about meeting requirements, not reaching the highest achievable standard.
whyNot.2: Exceeding expectations is not the test; fulfilling the requirements is.
whyNot.3: Approval is a quality responsibility, not the definition of quality.

A.q: What does product-based quality help a project to avoid?
options: Recording quality activities in the quality register
Setting quality tolerances for individual products
Effort on work not traceable to the business justification
Changing requirements after the PID has been formally baselined
A.why: Translating requirements into acceptance criteria and quality specifications for products helps avoid spending resources on work that cannot be traced back to the business justification (manual 8.1.2).

whyNot.0: Recording quality activities is part of quality control, which product-based quality supports.
whyNot.1: Quality tolerances are set for products; product-based quality does not avoid them.
whyNot.3: Requirements are expected to change; changes are handled through the issue management approach.

B.q:
Which two statements about the quality practice are correct?
1. It aims to ensure products meet requirements and expectations and enable the benefits.
2. Requirements should stay unchanged once captured in initiation.
3. Requirements are translated into acceptance criteria and quality specifications.
4. It defines the business justification for the project.
options: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
B.why: Quality is about products meeting requirements and expectations and enabling the benefits (1), and the product-based approach translates requirements into acceptance criteria and quality specifications (3).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is false: the team should expect requirements to change and be ready to handle the changes.
whyNot.2: Both are false: requirements will change, and the business justification belongs to the business case practice.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is false: the business case practice documents the justification.

B.q: A project board member says requirements captured during initiation must now be frozen for the rest of the project. What does the quality practice say?
options: Freezing them is correct once the PID is approved
Changes are allowed until the first delivery stage begins
The senior supplier decides whether requirements can change
The team should expect changes and be ready to handle them
B.why: However thoroughly requirements are captured, the project management team should anticipate requirement changes and be prepared to handle them (manual 8.1.2).

whyNot.0: Expecting requirements to remain unchanged is unrealistic; changes go through the issue management approach.
whyNot.1: There is no rule that changes stop at a particular stage.
whyNot.2: Changes are decided by the project board or a change authority, not the senior supplier.

B.q: Why does PRINCE2 link quality to the realization of benefits?
options: Quality tolerances are defined within the benefits management approach
The senior supplier is responsible for realizing the benefits
Products that fail requirements cannot enable the intended outcomes
Benefits are measured during quality control activities
B.why: Quality is concerned with ensuring the products meet the user's requirements and expectations and enable the desired benefits to be realized (manual 8.1).

whyNot.0: Quality tolerances come from acceptance criteria and quality specifications, not the benefits management approach.
whyNot.1: The senior user is responsible for specifying and realizing benefits, not the senior supplier.
whyNot.3: Quality control checks products against specifications; benefits are measured through the benefits management approach.

C.q: A team proposes adding an extra report screen. Which question best applies product-based quality, and which practice handles the change if it is wanted?
options: Which product and justification it supports; issues
How much the supplier would charge to build it; quality
Which stage it will be built in; plans
Whether the users would like it; organizing
C.why: Product-based quality asks whether work traces to a product and to the business justification; a change to baselined products is handled by the issues practice through the issue management approach.

whyNot.1: Cost matters, but product-based quality is about traceability, and changes are controlled by the issues practice.
whyNot.2: Scheduling is a plans question and does not test traceability; change control sits in the issues practice.
whyNot.3: Users liking a feature does not show traceability, and organizing does not control changes.

C.q: Which pairing correctly matches a practice to its purpose?
options: Quality: control changes to the project's baseline
Plans: document the user's requirements of the project's products
Quality: establish how the user's requirements will be met
Issues: define the means to deliver the products
C.why: The quality practice documents the user's requirements of the products and establishes the means by which they will be met.

whyNot.0: Controlling changes to the baseline is the issues practice.
whyNot.1: Documenting the user's requirements of the products is the quality practice.
whyNot.3: Defining the means to deliver the products is the plans practice.

C.q: A product meets all its agreed requirements but is simpler than a rival product. According to PRINCE2, what is its quality?
options: Poor, because the rival is more advanced
Acceptable once the supplier adds more features
Unknown until the benefits have been measured
Good, because it fulfils its requirements
C.why: Quality is the degree to which inherent characteristics fulfil requirements, so a product meeting its agreed requirements is of the required quality.

whyNot.0: Comparison with a rival is not the PRINCE2 test of quality.
whyNot.1: Adding unrequired features is gold-plating and cannot be traced to the justification.
whyNot.2: Benefits are measured separately; product quality is judged against requirements.

reteach.title: A made-to-measure suit
reteach.question: When is a suit from a tailor 'good quality'?

blocks.h: It fits what you asked for
blocks.body: You tell the tailor what you need: navy, two buttons, fits a 40-inch chest, ready for a wedding in May. The tailor notes it, then takes measurements and plans fittings so the result can be checked. A suit that matches your order and fits is good quality, even if it is not the most expensive cloth. That is the quality practice: record the requirements, then set up the means to meet and check them.

head: Tailor
Quality practice
rows: Establishes the means to meet them

blocks.text: A silk lining you never asked for does not make the suit better quality. It is work that cannot be traced to your requirements.

test.q: Identify the missing words in the following sentence. The quality practice documents the user's requirements of the project's products and [?] by which they will be met.
options: sets the tolerances
establishes the means
records the risks
approves the plans
test.why: The purpose is to document the user's requirements of the products and to establish the means by which they will be met.

whyNot.0: Tolerances are part of quality planning, not the wording of the purpose.
whyNot.2: Recording risks belongs to the risk practice.
whyNot.3: Approving plans is a project board decision, not the quality purpose.

explain.body: Quality is the degree to which inherent characteristics fulfil requirements, not the most impressive possible result.

test.q: What is a product's quality judged against in PRINCE2?
options: Its agreed requirements
Its competitors' features
Its supplier's reputation
Its final cost
test.why: Quality is the degree to which inherent characteristics fulfil requirements.

whyNot.1: Competitor features are not the test of quality.
whyNot.2: Reputation does not show whether this product meets its requirements.
whyNot.3: Cost is a separate performance target.

explain.body: Requirements become acceptance criteria and quality specifications for products, so every check traces to a product and to the justification.

test.q: Into what does PRINCE2's product-based approach translate requirements?
options: Work package descriptions and their team plans
Risk responses and contingent plans
Acceptance criteria and quality specifications
Stage boundaries and stage tolerances
test.why: The product-based approach translates requirements into acceptance criteria and quality specifications for the products and the activities that deliver them.

whyNot.0: Work packages and team plans are planning products derived later.
whyNot.1: Risk responses belong to the risk practice.
whyNot.3: Stage boundaries are a manage by stages concept.

explain.body: However well requirements are captured, expect them to change and be ready to handle the changes through the issue management approach.

test.q: What should the project management team assume about requirements captured in initiation?
options: They are fixed once captured
They are likely to change
They belong to the supplier
They replace the business case
test.why: The team should anticipate requirement changes and be prepared to handle them (manual 8.1.2).

whyNot.0: Expecting requirements to stay fixed is unrealistic.
whyNot.2: Requirements are the user's; the supplier delivers against them.
whyNot.3: Requirements support the business case; they do not replace it.
